# Why Compound Interest Outgrows Simple Interest (Socratic)

**Goal:** Explain, with numbers and pictures, why compound interest grows faster than simple interest.  
**Level:** High school · **Method:** Socratic (you reach each idea through questions) · **Lessons:** in the course app

> Generated from `course.json`. Edit the course through Claude, not this file.

## Course overview

**Why it matters.** Every savings account, loan and credit card follows one of two rules for interest, and over long periods the two rules lead to very different amounts of money. Knowing why they differ, and not only that they do, lets you judge an offer, a debt or a savings plan for yourself instead of trusting the advertised rate.

**What you will learn.** The course starts from the old question of what to do with unpaid interest (Lesson 1). It then builds four ideas in order: interest is a rate applied to a base (Lesson 2), a fixed base gives equal steps (Lesson 3), a base that takes in its own interest gives interest on interest (Lesson 4), and the gap between the two widens every period (Lesson 5). Four applications follow: many years in one calculation (Lesson 6), doubling times (Lesson 7), starting early against starting big (Lesson 8) and monthly rates on debt (Lesson 9). A final comparison of two real-looking offers (Lesson 10) puts everything into one explanation.

Four principles carry the course. *Interest is a share of a base*: a rate means nothing until you know what it is charged on. *Fixed base, equal steps*: charge always on the original sum and the total climbs a straight line. *Interest on interest*: leave the interest in, and it joins the base, so each period multiplies the balance. *Multiplying outruns adding*: the gap between the two is the interest earned by earlier interest, and it grows faster every period. The facts you rely on are few: what principal, simple interest and compounding mean, that rates are quoted per period, the Rule of 72 for doubling times, and which real products follow which rule.

**You will be able to:**
- Work out simple and compound interest year by year and in one calculation
- Point to the exact euros that make a compound balance larger than a simple one
- Explain in plain words, with a picture, why the gap between the two widens over time
- Estimate how long money or a debt takes to double
- Decide between a simple and a compound offer for a given time span and justify the choice

## The story

**Before.** For most of recorded history, interest was a fixed charge per period on the sum lent, paid as it fell due. What to do with interest that was not paid was a contested matter: some lenders added it to the debt, and several legal systems, Roman law among them, restricted that practice.

**The aha.** It matters what the rate is charged on: interest that is left in becomes part of the sum that earns the next interest.

**What it solved.** Long-term saving, lending and borrowing became calculable. Printed interest tables, in commercial use by the 1600s, let anyone find the value of a sum after many years, and the same reasoning now underlies savings accounts, loans, credit cards and pensions.

## Principles

| | Principle | Statement |
|---|---|---|
|  | Interest is a share of a base | The interest for one period is the rate multiplied by the amount it is charged on (the base): the rate alone says nothing until you know the base. |
|  | Fixed base, equal steps | When interest is always charged on the original sum, every period adds the same amount, so the total rises in equal steps along a straight line. |
| ★ | Interest on interest | When interest is added to the balance, it becomes part of the base, so the next period's interest is charged on the earlier interest too: each period multiplies the balance by the same factor. |
| ★ | Multiplying outruns adding | Simple interest adds the same amount each period and compound interest multiplies by the same factor; the gap between them is exactly the interest earned on earlier interest, and it grows by more in every period than in the one before. |

★ **Key ideas** are the hardest principles. Each one is taught through the aha moment and then level by level.
- **Interest on interest**: counter-intuitive, persistent misconception, load-bearing (6 later lessons need it)
- **Multiplying outruns adding**: counter-intuitive, persistent misconception, load-bearing (4 later lessons need it)

## Facts to know

| | Fact | Used in |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | The principal is the sum originally lent or deposited, before any interest. | Lesson 2, Lesson 3, Lesson 4, Lesson 5, Lesson 10 |
| F2 | An interest rate is quoted per period, per year unless stated otherwise, as a percentage; $r\,\% = r/100$ as a decimal. | Lesson 2, Lesson 3, Lesson 4, Lesson 6, Lesson 9 |
| F3 | "Simple interest" means by definition that the interest of every period is charged on the principal only. | Lesson 3, Lesson 5, Lesson 7, Lesson 8, Lesson 10 |
| F4 | "Compound interest" means by definition that the interest of each period is added to the balance at the end of that period (called compounding), once a year unless stated otherwise. | Lesson 4, Lesson 5, Lesson 6, Lesson 7, Lesson 8, Lesson 10 |
| F5 | Rule of 72: at $r\,\%$ compound interest per year, money doubles in roughly $72 / r$ years (a good approximation for rates between about 2% and 12%). | Lesson 7 |
| F6 | Savings accounts and credit cards compound: unpaid interest is added to the balance. A bond that pays its interest out to the holder each year behaves like simple interest, because the base never grows. | Lesson 3, Lesson 4, Lesson 9 |
| F7 | A credit card quotes a rate per month and adds unpaid interest to the balance every month, so a year has 12 compounding periods. | Lesson 9 |

## Background you need

- Finding a percentage of an amount and writing a percentage as a decimal
- Powers with whole-number exponents
- Using a calculator for powers
- Reading a straight-line graph
